summary.text: Writing the rising binomial coefficients as products, the proof compares the levels \(p^{s+1}\) and \(p^s\), splits indices into multiples of \(p\) and units, and pairs \(k\) with \(p^{s+1}-k\); second- and third-order product expansions then reduce the error terms to reciprocal-power sums whose reflection and Fermat congruences give valuation at least \(3s+6\) (with the sharper unit-sum bounds adjusted for \(p=3\)). A Vandermonde convolution isolates the boundary contribution, and the same product-pair cancellations bound it to the required order, so the whole difference is divisible by \(p^{3s+6}\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 b_M(k)=\binom{M+k-1}{k},\qquad c_M(k)=\binom{M+k}{k},
 \qquad f(x)=3x^2+2x^3.
\]
Thus
\[
 a(M)=\sum_{k=0}^{M}f(b_M(k)).
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\). All estimates below are in \(\mathbf Q_p\). We write
\[
 X=O(p^j)
\]
to mean \(v_p(X)\ge j\). We use freely the elementary nonarchimedean rules
\[
 O(p^i)+O(p^i)=O(p^i),\qquad O(p^i)O(p^j)=O(p^{i+j}),
\]
and the fact that an integer not divisible by \(p\), and its inverse, are \(O(1)\).

We prove the following equivalent assertion. For every \(s\ge1\),
\[
 a(p^{s+1})-a(p^s)=O(p^{3s+6}). \tag{1}
\]
Putting \(r=s+1\) then gives the desired modulus \(p^{3r+3}\).

Throughout, put
\[
 U_p(M)=\{i:0\le i<M,\ p\nmid i\},
 \qquad H_j(M)=\sum_{i\in U_p(M)}i^{-j}.
\]
If \(p\mid M\), reflection \(i\mapsto M-i\) permutes \(U_p(M)\). If \(M\) is odd, it identifies its two halves, so that
\[
 \sum_{i\in U_p(M)}F(i)
 =\sum_{\substack{i\in U_p(M)\\2i<M}}
       \bigl(F(i)+F(M-i)\bigr). \tag{2}
\]
We shall repeatedly use this without further comment.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Harmonic-sum estimates
--------------------------------------------------------------------

It is useful to handle \(p=3\) and \(p\ge5\) simultaneously. Define
\[
 e=\begin{cases}0,&p=3,\\1,&p\ge5.\end{cases}
\]
Then
\[
 e\le1,\qquad H_2(p)=O(p^e),\qquad 3=O(p^{1-e}). \tag{3}
\]
For \(p=3\), these are immediate. For \(p\ge5\), Fermat's congruence gives
\(i^{-2}\equiv i^{p-3}\pmod p\) for \(1\le i<p\), while the sum of the \((p-3)\)-rd powers over \(\mathbf F_p\) is zero because \(0<p-3<p-1\). Hence \(H_2(p)\equiv0\pmod p\), proving (3).

We need several standard expansions. If \(i\) and \(i+x\) are \(p\)-adic units and \(x=O(p^j)\), then
\[
 (i+x)^{-n}=i^{-n}-nxi^{-n-1}+O(p^{2j}), \tag{4}
\]
and, in the case \(n=2\),
\[
 (i+x)^{-2}=i^{-2}-2xi^{-3}+3x^2i^{-4}+O(p^{3j}). \tag{5}
\]
These follow by bringing the two sides to a common denominator; for example the error in (5) is
\[
 -\frac{x^3(4i+3x)}{i^4(i+x)^2}.
\]

Splitting \(U_p(p^{m+1})\) into the blocks \(i+p^m d\), with
\(i\in U_p(p^m)\) and \(0\le d<p\), and applying (4), gives, for \(m\ge1\),
\[
 H_{j+1}(p^{m+1})-pH_{j+1}(p^m)=O(p^{m+1}). \tag{6}
\]
For \(j=1\), use the more precise expansion (5). The linear term contains
\(p^m\sum_{d=0}^{p-1}d\), and the quadratic term contains
\(p^{2m}\sum d^2\). Since
\[
 \sum_{d=0}^{p-1}d=\frac{p(p-1)}2=O(p)
\]
and, for \(p\ge5\),
\[
 \sum_{d=0}^{p-1}d^2=\frac{p(p-1)(2p-1)}6=O(p),
\]
one obtains the refined recurrence
\[
 H_2(p^{m+1})-pH_2(p^m)=O(p^{m+1+e}). \tag{7}
\]
For \(p=3\), (6) is exactly the required version of (7), because then \(e=0\).

Iterating (7) yields
\[
 H_2(p^m)-p^{m-1}H_2(p)=O(p^{m+e}), \tag{8}
\]
and consequently
\[
 H_2(p^m)=O(p^{m+e-1}). \tag{9}
\]
More generally, splitting \(U_p(p^m u)\) into \(u\) blocks and using (4) gives
\[
 H_2(p^m u)-uH_2(p^m)=O(p^{2m}), \tag{10}
\]
so
\[
 H_2(p^m u)=O(p^{m+e-1}). \tag{11}
\]

Reflection supplies the corresponding estimates for \(H_1\). Pairing \(i\) and \(M-i\), one has the exact identity
\[
 2H_1(M)+MH_2(M)
 =M^2\sum_{i\in U_p(M)}\frac1{i^2(M-i)}. \tag{12}
\]
The sum on the right is \(O(M)\): indeed
\[
 \sum_{i\in U_p(M)}\frac1{i^2(M-i)}
 =-H_3(M)+M\sum_{i\in U_p(M)}\frac1{i^3(M-i)},
\]
and reflection shows \(H_3(M)=O(M)\). Since 2 is a unit, (12) gives
\[
 H_1(M)+\frac M2H_2(M)=O(M^3). \tag{13}
\]
With \(M=p^m u\), (11) and (13) imply
\[
 H_1(p^m u)=O(p^{2m+e-1}). \tag{14}
\]
A more precise use of (8), (10), and (13) gives
\[
 H_1(p^s u)
 =-\frac{u^2}{2}p^{2s-1}H_2(p)+O(p^{2s+e}). \tag{15}
\]
There is also a reflected difference form. From
\[
 H_1(m)-H_1(n-m)
 =n\sum_{j\in U_p(m)}\frac1{j(n-j)}-H_1(n),
\]
with \(n=p^{s+1}\), and from (8), (10), and (14), one obtains, for \(u\le p\),
\[
 H_1(p^su)-H_1(p^s(p-u))
 =-u p^{2s}H_2(p)+O(p^{2s+1+e}). \tag{16}
\]

For later summations define
\[
 \Lambda_m(k)=\sum_{j\in U_p(p^m)}(j+p^mk)^{-2}.
\]
Equations (9) and (4) imply
\[
 \Lambda_m(k)=O(p^{m+e-1}), \tag{17}
\]
and block decomposition gives the exact recursion
\[
 \Lambda_{m+1}(k)=\sum_{d=0}^{p-1}\Lambda_m(pk+d). \tag{18}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Binomial descent and reflection
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Define
\[
 \rho_{\ell,M}(m)=\prod_{i\in U_p(m)}\left(1+\frac{\ell M}{i}\right).
\]
Since
\[
 c_M(k)=\prod_{i=0}^{k}\left(1+\frac Mi\right)
\]
(the factor at \(i=0\) is interpreted as 1), separating the indices divisible by \(p\) gives the exact descent formula
\[
 c_{pN}(k)=c_N(\lfloor k/p\rfloor)\rho_{1,pN}(k+1). \tag{19}
\]
Thus, if \(k\ge1\),
\[
 b_{pN}(pk)=b_N(k)\rho_{1,pN}(pk), \tag{20}
\]
whereas if \(p\nmid k\),
\[
 b_{pN}(k)=\frac{pN}{k}\,c_N(\lfloor k/p\rfloor)\rho_{1,pN}(k). \tag{21}
\]
Also, for \(s\ge1\) and \(k<p^s\),
\[
 c_{p^s}(k)=1+O(p). \tag{22}
\]
Indeed every nontrivial factor in its product differs from 1 by a multiple of \(p\).

For reflection define
\[
 \Theta_M(k)=\prod_{j=k+1}^{M-k}\left(1-\frac{2M}{j}\right),
 \qquad \varepsilon_M(k)=1-\Theta_M(k).
\]
A repeated use of
\(b_M(j+1)=b_M(j)(M+j)/(j+1)\) proves that, when \(M\) is odd,
\(k\ge1\), and \(2k+1\le M\),
\[
 b_M(M-k)=-b_M(k)\Theta_M(k). \tag{23}
\]
In particular, if
\[
 D_M(k)=b_M(k)+b_M(M-k),
\]
then
\[
 D_M(k)=b_M(k)\varepsilon_M(k). \tag{24}
\]

A form of \(\varepsilon\) adapted to descent is obtained by pairing the factors in \(\Theta\). Put
\[
 \Psi_M(k)=\prod_{k<j<(M+1)/2}
 \left(1+\frac{2M^2}{j(M-j)}\right),
 \qquad \mu_M(k)=1-\Psi_M(k).
\]
Then
\[
 \Theta_M(k)=\left(1-\frac{2M}{M-k}\right)\Psi_M(k),

the pairing being the elementary identity
\[
 \left(1-\frac{2M}{j}\right)
 \left(1-\frac{2M}{M-j}\right)
 =1+\frac{2M^2}{j(M-j)}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 \varepsilon_M(k)=\frac{2M}{M-k}-\frac{M+k}{M-k}\mu_M(k). \tag{25}
\]
Each factor defining \(\Psi_{p^s}\) differs from 1 by \(O(p^2)\), even when its denominator contains powers of \(p\); hence
\[
 \mu_{p^s}(k)=O(p^2). \tag{26}
\]
More explicitly, if \(k=p^vu\), \(p\nmid u\), and \(v\le s\), then
\[
 b_{p^s}(k)=O(p^{s-v}). \tag{27}
\]
If in addition \(2k+1\le p^s\), then
\[
 \varepsilon_{p^s}(k)=O(p^t)
 \quad(t\le2,\ v+t\le s), \tag{28}
\]
and therefore, by (24),
\[
 D_{p^s}(k)=O(p^{s-v+t}). \tag{29}
\]
To see (27), write \(b_{p^s}(k)=p^s c_{p^s}(k-1)/k\). For (28), note that \(p^s-k\) has the same \(p\)-adic valuation as \(k\), and use (25) and (26). The case where \(k\) lies in the upper half follows by replacing it with \(p^s-k\).

For descent of \(\mu\), define
\[
 \Phi_N(k)=\prod_{\substack{k<j<(pN+1)/2\\p\nmid j}}
 \left(1+\frac{2(pN)^2}{j(pN-j)}\right).
\]
If \(k=pk'+k_0\), \(0\le k_0<p\), then separating multiples of \(p\) gives
\[
 \Psi_{pN}(k)=\Psi_N(k')\Phi_N(k),

the endpoints matching because \(N\) is odd. Thus
\[
 \mu_{pN}(k)=\mu_N(k')+(1-\mu_N(k'))(1-\Phi_N(k)). \tag{30}
\]
For \(N=p^s\), every factor in \(\Phi_N\) differs from 1 by
\(O(p^{2s+2})\), so
\[
 1-\Phi_{p^s}(k)=O(p^{2s+2}). \tag{31}
\]

We also require the second-order product expansion
\[
 2\left(\rho_{\ell,M}(m)-1-\ell M H_1(m)\right)
 = (\ell M H_1(m))^2-(\ell M)^2H_2(m)+O(M^3). \tag{32}
\]
This is just
\(\prod(1+x_i)=1+\sum x_i+\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j+O(x^3)\), together with
\(2\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j=(\sum x_i)^2-\sum x_i^2\).

Combining (32) with (14)--(16) gives three estimates that will drive the multiple-of-\(p\) part. For \(v\le s\),
\[
 \rho_{1,p^{s+1}}(p^{v+1}u)-1
   =O(p^{s+2+e+2v}), \tag{33}
\]
and if
\(p^{s+1}-p^{v+1}u=p^{v+1}u'\), then
\[
 \rho_{1,p^{s+1}}(p^{v+1}u)
 -\rho_{1,p^{s+1}}(p^{v+1}u')
 =O(p^{2s+2+v+e}). \tag{34}
\]
At the deepest level \(v=s-1\), the leading terms must be retained. Writing \(h=H_2(p)\), (15), (16), and (32) give
\[
 \rho_{1,p^{s+1}}(p^su)-1
 =-\frac{u^2}{2}p^{3s}h+O(p^{3s+1+e}), \tag{35}
\]
\[
 \rho_{1,p^{s+1}}(p^su)
 -\rho_{1,p^{s+1}}(p^s(p-u))
 =-2up^{3s+1}h+O(p^{3s+2+e}). \tag{36}
\]
Finally, iterating (20) and using (33) shows
\[
 b_{p^s}(p^{s-1}u)=b_p(u)+O(p^3). \tag{37}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Rewriting the sum
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Define
\[
 g(x,y)=3x^2(x+y)+\frac32(x+y)^2-3x(x+y)^2+(x+y)^3.
\]
A direct expansion gives
\[
 g(x,y)+g(y,x)=f(x)+f(y)+6xy. \tag{38}
\]
Vandermonde's identity gives
\[
 3\sum_{k=0}^{M}b_M(k)b_M(M-k)=2c_{2M}(M). \tag{39}
\]
Also \(b_M(M)=c_M(M)/2\). Pairing the summands in \(a(M)\), using (38) and (39), yields
\[
 a(M)=B(M)+\sum_{1\le k<M}G_M(k), \tag{40}
\]
where
\[
 G_M(k)=g(b_M(k),b_M(M-k))
\]
and
\[
 B(M)=5+f(c_M(M)/2)+3c_M(M)-2c_{2M}(M). \tag{41}
\]

Take \(N=p^s\). Split the interior indices for \(pN\) into multiples and nonmultiples of \(p\). Pair the latter by \(k\leftrightarrow pN-k\), and use (23)--(24). One gets the exact decomposition
\[
\begin{split}
 a(pN)-a(N)={}&B(pN)-B(N)\\
 &+\sum_{\substack{p\nmid k\\1\le k<(pN+1)/2}}U_{pN}(k)\\
 &+\sum_{k'=1}^{N-1}\bigl(G_{pN}(pk')-G_N(k')\bigr), \tag{42}
\end{split}
\]
where, with \(x=b_M(k)\) and \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon_M(k)\),
\[
 U_M(k)=x^2\varepsilon
 \bigl(3\varepsilon+6x-6x\varepsilon+2x\varepsilon^2\bigr). \tag{43}
\]
We estimate the three lines of (42) separately.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. The nonmultiples of \(p\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Put \(n=p^{s+1}\). For \(p\nmid k\), (21), (22), and (30) give
\[
 b_n(k)=\frac nk\,c_{p^s}(\lfloor k/p\rfloor)\rho_{1,n}(k), \tag{44}
\]
\[
 \varepsilon_n(k)=\frac{2n}{n-k}
 -\frac{n+k}{n-k}\left(\mu_{p^s}(\lfloor k/p\rfloor)+\delta_k\right), \tag{45}
\]
where
\[
 \delta_k=(1-\mu_{p^s}(\lfloor k/p\rfloor))(1-\Phi_{p^s}(k)).
\]
Here
\[
 n=O(p^{s+1}),\quad c_{p^s}(\lfloor k/p\rfloor)-1=O(p),
\quad \rho_{1,n}(k)-1=O(p^{s+1}),
\]
\[
 \mu_{p^s}(\lfloor k/p\rfloor)=O(p^2),
\quad \delta_k=O(p^{2s+2}),
\quad \varepsilon_n(k)=O(p^2). \tag{46}
\]
All denominators involving \(k\) and \(n-k\) are units.

Two aggregate estimates result:
\[
 \sum_{\substack{p\nmid k\\k<(n+1)/2}}b_n(k)^3\varepsilon_n(k)
   =O(p^{3s+6}), \tag{47}
\]
\[
 \sum_{\substack{p\nmid k\\k<(n+1)/2}}b_n(k)^2\varepsilon_n(k)^2
   =O(p^{3s+5+e}). \tag{48}
\]
We now justify these, including the summation cancellations that are not visible termwise.

Substitute (44)--(45) into the left side of (47), factor out \(n^3\), and expand. Every term containing \(\rho^3-1\), \(\delta_k\), or an additional factor \(n\mu\) is already \(O(p^3)\) inside the remaining sum. The two potentially smaller sums reduce to
\[
 2n\sum \frac{c^3}{(n-k)k^3},
 \qquad
 \sum \frac{c^3\mu}{k^3}. \tag{49}
\]
For \(s>1\), the first is termwise \(O(p^3)\). For \(s=1\), write it as
\[
 -2n\sum k^{-4}
 +2n\sum\frac{k(c^3-1)+n}{(n-k)k^4}.
\]
The second sum is termwise \(O(p^3)\), while
\[
 \sum_{\substack{p\nmid k\\k<(p^2+1)/2}}k^{-4}=O(p). \tag{50}
\]
Indeed reflection converts twice this half-sum into \(H_4(p^2)\), up to an \(O(p)\) error; and (6) gives \(H_4(p^2)=O(p)\).

For the second expression in (49), restore the reflected half, noting that \(\mu_{p^s}(\lfloor(n-k)/p\rfloor)=0\) on the reflected half. Split \(k=pk'+k_0\). Pairing the inner residues \(k_0\leftrightarrow p-k_0\) shows
\[
 \sum_{k_0\in U_p(p)}(pk'+k_0)^{-3}=O(p).
\]
Together with \(\mu=O(p^2)\), this gives the necessary \(O(p^3)\). This proves (47).

For (48), substitution of (44)--(45) and extraction of \(n^2\) leaves four types of terms. Those containing \(\rho^2-1\), \(\delta_k\), or extra powers of \(n\) are termwise
\(O(p^{s+3+e})\). The pure rational term is handled as above; when \(s=1\), (50) supplies the extra factor \(p\). The term linear in \(\mu\) again uses the inverse-cube residue pairing. The remaining term is
\[
 \sum_{k'=0}^{p^s-1}c_{p^s}(k')^2\mu_{p^s}(k')^2\Lambda_1(k'). \tag{51}
\]
The following inductive estimate completes the argument:
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{p^t-1}c_{p^t}(k)^2\mu_{p^t}(k)^2\Lambda_m(k)
 =O(p^{t+m+2+e}) \quad(t,m\ge1). \tag{52}
\]
For \(t=1\), this follows from \(\mu=O(p^2)\) and (17). For the induction step write \(k=pk'+k_0\), apply (19), (30), and (18). The main term is exactly the assertion at level \(t-1\) with \(m+1\). Every correction contains at least one of
\(\rho-1=O(p^t)\), \(\mu=O(p^2)\), or
\(1-\Phi=O(p^{2t})\), and (17) supplies the remaining valuation. This proves (52), hence (48).

Now expand (43) as
\[
 U_n(k)=3b_n(k)^2\varepsilon_n(k)^2
 +6b_n(k)^3\varepsilon_n(k)
 +b_n(k)^3\varepsilon_n(k)^2(2\varepsilon_n(k)-6). \tag{53}
\]
The first sum is \(O(p^{3s+6})\) by (48) and
\(3=O(p^{1-e})\); the second is so by (47). In the last sum,
\(b_n(k)=O(p^{s+1})\) and \(\varepsilon_n(k)=O(p^2)\), so it is termwise \(O(p^{3s+7})\). Thus
\[
 \sum_{\substack{p\nmid k\\k<(n+1)/2}}U_n(k)=O(p^{3s+6}). \tag{54}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. The multiples of \(p\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

By (20), if \(1\le k'<p^s\), then
\[
 G_{p^{s+1}}(pk')
 =g(x\rho_1,y\rho_2), \tag{55}
\]
where
\[
 x=b_{p^s}(k'),\quad y=b_{p^s}(p^s-k'),

after writing \(k'=p^vu\), \(p\nmid u\),
\[
 \rho_1=\rho_{1,p^{s+1}}(p^{v+1}u),
 \quad
 \rho_2=\rho_{1,p^{s+1}}(p^{v+1}u'),

aud \(p^s-p^vu=p^vu'\).

First suppose \(v+2\le s\). By (27), (29), (33), and (34),
\[
 x,y=O(p^{s-v}),\quad x+y=O(p^{s-v+2}), \tag{56}
\]
\[
 \rho_1-1,\rho_2-1=O(p^{s+2+e+2v}),
 \quad \rho_1-\rho_2=O(p^{2s+2+v+e}). \tag{57}
\]
Set \(D=x+y\), \(a=\rho_1-1\), \(b=\rho_2-1\), and
\[
 W=x(a-b)+Db.
\]
Then
\[
 x\rho_1+y\rho_2=D+W,
 \qquad W=O(p^{2s+4+e+v}).
\]
Expanding the defining polynomial \(g\), one finds
\[
\begin{split}
 g(x(1+a),y(1+b))-g(x,y)
={}&3\{x^2(2a+a^2)(D+W)+x^2W\}\\
&+\frac32W(2D+W)\\
&-3\{xa(D+W)^2+xW(2D+W)\}\\
&+W(3D^2+3DW+W^2).
\end{split} \tag{58}
\]
Substitution of (56)--(57) into every displayed monomial shows that each is \(O(p^{3s+6})\). Therefore
\[
 G_{p^{s+1}}(pk')-G_{p^s}(k')=O(p^{3s+6})
 \quad(v+2\le s). \tag{59}
\]

It remains to handle the deepest indices
\(k'=p^{s-1}u\), \(1\le u<p\). These cannot be estimated termwise without retaining the leading terms (35)--(36). Put
\[
 x=b_{p^s}(p^{s-1}u),\quad
 y=b_{p^s}(p^{s-1}(p-u)),
\]
\[
 x_0=b_p(u),\qquad D_0=b_p(u)+b_p(p-u),\qquad h=H_2(p).
\]
Then (29) and (37) give
\[
 x=O(p),\quad x+y=O(p^2),\quad x-x_0=O(p^3),
 \quad x+y-D_0=O(p^3). \tag{60}
\]
Using (35)--(36) in the full expansion of \(g(x\rho_1,y\rho_2)-g(x,y)\), and then replacing \(x,x+y\) by \(x_0,D_0\) using (60), gives
\[
\begin{split}
&G_{p^{s+1}}(p^su)-G_{p^s}(p^{s-1}u)\\
&\quad=-\frac32hp^{3s}T_u
 +9hp^{3s+4}u^{-2}+O(p^{3s+6}), \tag{61}
\end{split}
\]
where
\[
\begin{split}
T_u={}&3u^2x_0^2D_0+4pux_0^3+4pux_0D_0+u^2D_0^2
       +6p^4u^{-2}. \tag{62}
\end{split}
\]
For completeness, the algebra behind (61) is as follows. Write
\(a=\rho_1-1\), \(b=\rho_2-1\),
\(D=x+y\), and \(W=x(a-b)+Db\). In the expansion of \(g\), the terms linear in \(a,b,W\) are
\[
 2x^2D\,a+x^3(a-b)+x^2D\,b+xD(a-b)+D^2b.
\]
Insert
\(a,b\equiv-u^2p^{3s}h/2\) and
\(a-b\equiv-2up^{3s+1}h\) from (35)--(36). This produces
\(-hp^{3s}/2\) times the first four terms in (62). All quadratic and cubic terms have valuation at least \(3s+6\), using (60), (3), and \(e\le1\). The replacement of \(x,D\) by \(x_0,D_0\) costs \(O(p^5)\) in the bracket and hence also lies in \(O(p^{3s+6})\). The compensating last two terms in (61)--(62) are inserted so that the following level-\(p\) identity can be applied.

At level \(p\), reflection gives the sharper congruence
\[
 D_0=-2p^2u^{-2}+O(p^3). \tag{63}
\]
Indeed use (24)--(26), write
\(x_0=(p/u)c_p(u-1)\), and use \(c_p(u-1)=1+O(p)\); reflection covers the upper half. Substitution of (63) and
\(x_0=(p/u)(1+O(p))\) into (62) yields
\[
 T_u=-6p^4u^{-2}+O(p^5). \tag{64}
\]
This is a genuine cancellation among the four polynomial terms in (62), not merely a termwise estimate.

Summing (61) over \(u=1,\dots,p-1\), equation (64) makes the first main term \(O(p^{3s+6})\): its error contributes
\(h p^{3s}O(p^5)\), multiplied by \(3/2\), and (3) supplies the missing factor when \(p=3\). The explicitly displayed term also sums to \(O(p^{3s+6})\), because
\[
 \sum_{u=1}^{p-1}u^{-2}=H_2(p)=h

aud \(9h^2p^{3s+4}=O(p^{3s+6})\) by (3). Consequently the deepest stratum is \(O(p^{3s+6})\). Together with (59), this proves
\[
 \sum_{k'=1}^{p^s-1}
 \bigl(G_{p^{s+1}}(pk')-G_{p^s}(k')\bigr)
 =O(p^{3s+6}). \tag{65}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. The boundary term
--------------------------------------------------------------------

From (19), with the harmless endpoint removed,
\[
 c_{pN}(pN)=c_N(N)\rho_{1,pN}(pN),
\]
\[
 c_{2pN}(pN)=c_{2N}(N)\rho_{2,pN}(pN). \tag{66}
\]
Put, for \(N=p^s\),
\[
 C=c_N(N),\quad D=c_{2N}(N),\quad
 \rho_1=\rho_{1,pN}(pN),\quad \rho_2=\rho_{2,pN}(pN).
\]
We require three estimates.

First, (32) and (14) give
\[
 \rho_1-1=O(p^{3s+2+e}). \tag{67}
\]
Second, pair the factors in \(\rho_{\ell,pN}(pN)\). If
\[
 w_i=\frac{(pN)^2}{i(pN-i)},
\]
then
\[
 \rho_{\ell,pN}(pN)
 =\prod_{\substack{i\in U_p(pN)\\2i<pN}}
  \bigl(1+\ell(\ell+1)w_i\bigr). \tag{68}
\]
Here \(w_i=O(p^{2s+2})\), and
\[
 \sum w_i=pN\,H_1(pN)=O(p^{3s+2+e}). \tag{69}
\]
A second-order product expansion of (68), used for \(\ell=1,2\), gives
\[
 \rho_2-1-3(\rho_1-1)=O(p^{3s+6}). \tag{70}
\]
For \(s>1\), this follows termwise from \(w_i^2\). When \(s=1\), the needed additional factor follows from the half-sum estimate (50), because \(w_i^2\) is \(p^8\) times an inverse-fourth-power sum. This is the only delicate case in (70).

Third, define
\[
 K(C,D)=3C+\frac32C^2+\frac34C^3-6D.
\]
Then
\[
 K(C,D)=O(p^{4-e}). \tag{71}
\]
To prove this, first note from (66), (67), and its \(\ell=2\) analogue that both \(C=c_{p^s}(p^s)\) and \(D=c_{2p^s}(p^s)\) are stable modulo \(p^4\) as \(s\) varies. It is therefore enough to check (71) at level \(p\). If \(p=3\),
\[
 c_3(3)=20,
 \qquad c_6(3)=84,
\]
and
\[
 3\cdot20+\frac32\,20^2+\frac34\,20^3-6\cdot84
 =3^4\cdot76.
\]
If \(p\ge5\), then by (66) at \(N=1\),
\[
 c_p(p)=2\rho_{1,p}(p),\qquad c_{2p}(p)=3\rho_{2,p}(p),

aud (32), (3), and (14) show
\(\rho_{1,p}(p)-1,\rho_{2,p}(p)-1=O(p^3)\). Expanding \(K\) about \((C,D)=(2,3)\) therefore gives \(K=O(p^3)=O(p^{4-e})\). This proves (71).

Now use (41), (66), and set \(a=\rho_1-1\). A direct polynomial expansion gives
\[
\begin{split}
 B(pN)-B(N)={}&aK(C,D)
 -2D\bigl(\rho_2-1-3a\bigr)\\
 &+a^2\left(3(C/2)^2+6(C/2)^3\right)
 +2(C/2)^3a^3. \tag{72}
\end{split}
\]
The first term is \(O(p^{3s+6})\) by (67) and (71); the second is so by (70); and the last two are so by (67), since \(C,D\) are integral. Hence
\[
 B(p^{s+1})-B(p^s)=O(p^{3s+6}). \tag{73}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Completion
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Insert (54), (65), and (73) into the exact decomposition (42). All three contributions are \(O(p^{3s+6})\), so
\[
 a(p^{s+1})-a(p^s)=O(p^{3s+6}).
\]
Both values of \(a\) are integers. For an integer, being \(O(p^m)\) in \(\mathbf Q_p\) is equivalent to divisibility by \(p^m\). Thus
\[
 a(p^{s+1})\equiv a(p^s)\pmod{p^{3s+6}}.
\]
Finally, given \(r\ge2\), put \(s=r-1\ge1\). Then
\[
 3s+6=3(r-1)+6=3r+3,
\]
and therefore
\[
 \boxed{a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod{p^{3r+3}}}.
\]
This holds for every prime \(p\ge3\), as required.
